title: Animal Aggressions with Rabies-Transmission Potential in Risaralda, Colombia, 2016–2026: Rising Severe Exposures and a Shifting Aggressor Profile
content: Background: Animal aggressions with rabies-transmission potential remain an important public health concern, requiring effective surveillance and timely post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). This study aimed to characterize temporal trends, epidemiological patterns, aggressor species, exposure severity, and clinical management of animal aggressions in Risaralda, Colombia, between 2016 and 2026. Methods: A retrospective, descriptive, ecological time-series study was conducted using records notified to Colombia’s National Public Health Surveillance System (SIVIGILA, event 300) from 2016 through epidemiological week 46 of 2026. Demographic characteristics, aggressor species, injury characteristics, animal observability, exposure classification, and PEP administration were analyzed. Temporal trends were estimated using quasi-Poisson regression, while categorical variables were compared using chi-square tests. Concordance between initial and final exposure classifications was assessed using weighted kappa statistics. Results: Overall, 41,419 notifications were analyzed. Annual notifications increased by 59%, from 3,041 in 2016 to 4,829 in 2025, with an annual percentage change of 4.5% (95% CI: 1.9–7.1). Median age was 28 years, and 51.8% were male. Dogs accounted for 80.4% of aggressions, followed by cats (18.3%), whose contribution increased from 15.6% to 22.2%. Severe exposures increased from 7.1% in 2016 to 16.5% in 2025, reaching 18.0% in 2026. Unobservable aggressor animals increased from 20.2% to 33.8% between 2016 and 2025. Rabies vaccination was administered in 99.4% of severe exposures and antirabies serum in 94.9%. Initial and final exposure classifications agreed in 85.9% of comparable records (weighted κ = 0.83). Conclusions: Animal aggression notifications increased substantially in Risaralda, accompanied by a disproportionate rise in severe exposure classifications, increasing feline involvement, and reduced animal observability. These findings highlight the need to strengthen integrated One Health surveillance, domestic animal vaccination, standardized exposure assessment, and timely PEP management.
